chunks: As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa, from Sama'a ibn Mihran, from Abu Basir:
He said: I asked him about a kurr of water I passed during travel, in which a donkey, a mule, or a person had urinated. He said: 'Do not perform wudu from it, and do not drink from it.'

The correct approach to this narration is to interpret it as applicable when one of the water's characteristics has changed — either its taste, its colour, or its smell. As for when that is absent [i.e., none of the properties have changed], there is no harm in using it, in accordance with the preceding narrations. And what points to this meaning is...

key_terms.أَوْصَافِ: characteristics (of water) — the three legally decisive properties: taste, colour, smell
key_terms.الْأَوَّلَةِ: the preceding/earlier — classical form of الأُولَى, referring to earlier narrations cited in the same chapter
key_terms.فَلَا بَأْسَ: there is no harm/objection — standard jurisprudential formula signifying permissibility
key_terms.كُرٍّ: kurr — the jurisprudentially fixed minimum volume of water (~377 litres) that in Shia fiqh resists impurity unless its properties change

ai.seo_question: What is the Shia jurisprudential ruling on using a kurr of water that has been urinated in by an animal or person?
ai.summary: Abu Basir asked an Imam (peace be upon him) about a kurr of water encountered during travel in which a donkey, mule, or person had urinated, and received the ruling not to perform wudu from it nor drink it. Shaykh al-Tusi reconciles this narration with other hadith in the chapter by confining the prohibition to cases where the water's organoleptic properties (taste, colour, or smell) have changed; where the water remains unaltered, using it is permissible per the earlier narrations.
